item.title: Five days inside the contradictions of the United Nations. [ dawn ]
item.description:
UNITED NATIONS: Only at the United Nations can a journalist walk through a corridor and suddenly find himself face to face with a prime minister, pause before a sculpture symbolising peace, read the words of a Persian poet written on a wall, and then rush outside to report on a protest against a war thousands of miles away.

For five days, I lived inside that extraordinary contradiction while covering the high-level debate of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. The official high-level week brought heads of state and government from around the world to the UN headquarters between September 22 and 26.

The first thing one begins to notice at the United Nations is the art.

There are sculptures, statues and works donated by countries that seem to confront you at every turn. They are reminders of peace, humanity, war and the hope that nations can somehow learn to live together.

Even before you enter the United Nations, the place begins to tell its story.

As you approach the Secretariat Building, you encounter Barbara Hepworth’s Single Form, the large abstract bronze standing beside the circular pool. Donated by Jacob Blaustein, it rises quietly against the building, its simple, powerful shape inviting a visitor to pause before entering a place where the world’s conflicts are debated.

Nearby stands St. George Slaying the Dragon, a sculpture presented to the United Nations by the Soviet Union. The familiar image of St. George defeating the dragon takes on a different meaning here, surrounded by the flags and institutions of an organisation created in the aftermath of war.

And then there is Antun Augustinčić’s Peace Monument, the mounted figure holding a sword and an olive branch. The Yugoslav/Croatian sculptor had wanted its silhouette to be visible from the East River, so that the idea of peace could announce itself even before a visitor reached the building.

Further along is Carl Fredrik Reuterswärd’s Non-Violence, the bronze revolver with its barrel tied into a knot, a gift from Luxembourg. Nearby, Evgeniy Vuchetich’s Let Us Beat Swords into Ploughshares shows a man transforming a sword into a tool for cultivating the earth.

Taken together, these sculptures seem to form a kind of preface to the United Nations: the human figure, the struggle against violence, the rejection of weapons and the hope that instruments of destruction can be transformed into instruments of peace.

And then you enter the building, where the symbols continue. On an entrance are the words of the great Persian poet Saadi, reminding us that human beings are parts of one body, created from the same essence — and that when one part suffers, the others cannot remain at peace.

And then, inside the building, you encounter the words of Saadi, the great Persian poet, written on a wall.

His famous lines describe human beings as parts of one body, created from the same essence. When one part suffers, the others cannot remain at peace.

I kept returning to those words during these five days.

Because almost everywhere I looked, I saw the world struggling with the very idea they express.

Iran and the United States were at the centre of intense diplomatic activity. Gaza dominated conversations inside the building and protests outside it. The war in Ukraine continued to draw attention, while India and Pakistan brought their familiar confrontation to the international forum.

The United Nations seemed to contain the whole contradiction of our age: an institution built on the idea that humanity can act together, confronted every day by evidence of how difficult that remains.

Outside the gates, protesters gathered in large numbers as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived to address the UN General Assembly. Inside, delegations walked out during his speech.

And there I was, moving between the demonstrations, the diplomatic meetings, the press conferences and the Assembly hall, doing what journalists do — watching, listening, asking questions and trying to understand what was happening behind the carefully prepared language of diplomacy.

At one point, I actually bumped into Netanyahu.

It was not a planned interview or a formal meeting. It was simply one of those extraordinary moments possible only at the United Nations, where presidents, prime ministers, diplomats, security officers, journalists and interpreters are constantly crossing one another’s paths.

The security arrangements themselves became part of the story.

During the US president’s stay in New York, security around the United Nations was extraordinarily tight. Motorcades moved through sealed streets, access was restricted and every movement of a major leader seemed choreographed. The arrival of leaders such as the Syrian and Turkish presidents added to the atmosphere.

Then the intensity would ease.

A major leader would leave, the barricades would move, the corridors would become less crowded, and suddenly the United Nations would feel almost ordinary again—until another motorcade arrived.

That rhythm is something a television broadcast cannot quite capture.

At the UN, diplomacy is not only what leaders say from the podium. It is also the waiting, the corridors, the security checks, the hurried whispers, the chance encounters and the small conversations between meetings.

Pakistan’s diplomatic role was another important part of my coverage.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Assembly as Islamabad continued efforts to facilitate dialogue between Iran and the United States. Shehbaz later said Pezeshkian regarded the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding as fully acceptable to Iran and was prepared to move it forward.

That is the other side of covering the UN.

You see confrontation, but you also see countries trying to create channels through which confrontation might be reduced.

And sometimes the most memorable moments have nothing to do with the major powers.

Only at the United Nations could I find myself in a photograph with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman of Bangladesh, Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua of Tonga and Deputy Prime Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioo of Samoa.

Three leaders from three very different parts of the world, standing together in New York.

Only at the United Nations.

The photograph captures something that statistics cannot. The General Assembly has 193 member states, each represented with one vote. Yet the world represented inside that building is vastly more complicated than a list of countries and votes.

Every delegation carries its own history. Every leader brings his country’s anxieties. Every journalist arrives carrying questions.

And outside, the protesters carry their anger.

For five days, I walked past the sculptures and statues, past the flags and security barriers, past presidents and prime ministers, past demonstrations and diplomatic receptions.

And each time I saw Saadi’s words on the wall, they seemed to ask the same simple question:

If we really are parts of one body, how can one part suffer while the rest remains at peace?

The United Nations has no easy answer. Perhaps that is why the question is still written on its wall.

And perhaps that is why, after five days of covering the world’s most powerful people, the image I carry with me is not of a speech or a motorcade.

It is of people from Bangladesh, Tonga, Samoa and Pakistan standing together for a photograph.

Only at the United Nations.

When will Bangla take its place at the UN?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There are moments in a nation's history when a language becomes much more than a means of communication. It becomes a symbol of identity, dignity, and collective struggle. For Bangladesh, Bangla is precisely such a language.
The blood shed during the Language Movement of 1952 transformed the demand for linguistic rights into one of the defining chapters of the nation's history. More than seven decades later, the question is no longer whether Bangla has a place in the global linguistic landscape. It is whether that place can now be reflected in the world's foremost multilateral institution -- the United Nations.
The United Nations began its journey in 1945 with five official languages: English, French, Russian, Spanish, and Mandarin (Chinese). Arabic was added in 1973, bringing the total number of official UN languages to six. Initially, only English and French were used as the working languages of the Security Council from 1946. Russian and Spanish were added in 1969, while Mandarin was adopted for that purpose in 1974. Although Arabic became an official UN language in 1973, its use in the Security Council began only in 1982.
Spanish is the official language of 20 countries worldwide, most of which are located in Latin America -- specifically Central America, the Caribbean, and South America. However, although Spanish is widely spoken in the United States, it is not the country's federal official language.
The history of these languages offers an important perspective on the question of Bangla. Russian and Spanish waited 23 years after the establishment of the United Nations before becoming Security Council languages, while Mandarin waited 29 years. Arabic, by contrast, was adopted as a Security Council language nine years after becoming an official UN language.
The official languages of all five permanent members of the Security Council (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) are also UN languages. At the same time, no Arab country or Muslim-majority member of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) has yet secured a permanent seat on the Security Council.
Although Bangla ranks sixth worldwide in terms of the number of speakers, it enjoys official-language status in only a limited number of jurisdictions. Russian, ranking eighth, has attained official UN language status, bypassing Bangla (ranked sixth) and Portuguese (ranked seventh).
Historically, imperial powers extended the influence of their languages in tandem with the expansion of their empires. Today, four European languages are among the official languages of the United Nations, while English serves as the official language of both the United Kingdom and the United States. Arabic, meanwhile, holds official status in numerous countries across Africa and the Middle East. Against this historical and geopolitical backdrop, the inclusion of another major Asian language remains an unresolved issue.
Bangladesh's heads of state or heads of government deliver speeches in Bangla at the United Nations General Assembly every year. Bangla's international profile received a major boost in 1999, when UNESCO proclaimed February 21 International Mother Language Day. What began as a commemoration of the language martyrs of Bangladesh has since become a global observance of linguistic diversity and the right to speak one's mother tongue.
The recognition gave Bangladesh a unique opportunity to place Bangla within a broader international discourse on language, culture, and identity. Yet international recognition and institutional recognition are not the same thing.
The price of recognition
One of the most frequently cited obstacles to making Bangla an official UN language is cost. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has previously indicated that Bangladesh would need to commit at least $60 million annually to meet the additional expenses, particularly for translation and interpretation within the UN system.
By comparison, Bangladesh currently contributes approximately $300,000 a year to the UN budget, or around 0.1% of the total.
The financial challenge is therefore substantial. But technology may have changed the nature of that challenge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed machine translation at a speed that would have been difficult to imagine even a decade ago.
The UN's enormous volume of documents, reports, statements, and communications requires translation between its six official languages. Extending such services to Bangla would undoubtedly require considerable investment, technical safeguards, and human oversight.
But the development of AI-assisted translation systems could potentially reduce the recurring cost substantially. Instead of viewing the $60 million figure as an unavoidable permanent expenditure, Bangladesh could explore whether an initial investment in research, development, language datasets, and AI-powered translation infrastructure could create a more sustainable model.
Such a system would still require professional translators and institutional quality control, particularly for diplomatic, legal, and technical documents. But technology could make the financial equation considerably more manageable.
This is where Bangladesh's growing information technology sector could become strategically important. The issue, therefore, should not be framed solely as a question of how much Bangladesh would have to pay. It should also be framed as a question of how Bangladesh can use its technological capabilities to reduce the cost of linguistic inclusion.
A language of more than 350 million people
The demographic case for Bangla is substantial. More than 350 million people around the world speak Bangla, placing it among the world's major languages. Yet the number of speakers alone does not determine whether a language becomes an official UN language.
Hindi, for example, has hundreds of millions of speakers but is not an official UN language. Russian, despite having considerably fewer speakers, already enjoys official status.
India's linguistic structure also makes a direct comparison between Hindi and Bangla more complicated. India has no single national language. The Constitution recognizes 22 languages, while individual states have their own official languages and English continues to play a major role in administration, higher education, and interstate communication.
Of course, international linguistic influence depends on much more than population. Political reach, economic relevance, geographic distribution, cultural influence, diplomatic utility, and institutional capacity all matter. That is why the question of Bangla's future at the UN cannot be reduced to a simple calculation of how many people speak it.
Bangla beyond Bangladesh
Bangla's geographical reach is far greater than Bangladesh alone. In addition to being the principal language of Bangladesh, Bangla is widely spoken in India, particularly in West Bengal, Tripura and Assam, as well as in other parts of eastern India.
Bangla-speaking communities also exist in Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Myanmar. Large Bangladeshi and Bangla-speaking communities have emerged across the Middle East, particularly in the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Qatar.
Beyond Asia and the Middle East, Bangla is spoken by substantial communities in the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Germany, Australia, and Japan. This global diaspora represents an important but underutilized resource for the internationalisation of Bangla.
For millions of expatriate Bengalis, Bangla remains the language of family, culture, and community. Over the past 25 years, Bangladeshi expatriate organizations in different cities around the world have submitted memoranda to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, Bangladesh's diplomatic missions, and the United Nations, calling for Bangla to be recognized as an official UN language.
What appears to be missing is a sustained, coordinated international campaign bringing these individual efforts together under a clearly defined national strategy.
Portuguese presents another useful comparison. With a global population of speakers broadly comparable to Bengali, Portuguese is used across at least 12 countries, including Portugal and Brazil, and has an established presence alongside Spanish across Europe, Latin America, and other parts of the world.
Malay is another language with a substantial regional footprint. It is spoken in Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Brunei, Timor-Leste, and parts of Thailand.
Arabic offers perhaps the most relevant precedent. It became an official UN language after the Arab states concerned agreed to shoulder the full cost of translating UN documents into Arabic.
Its recognition was therefore supported not simply by the number of speakers but by a coordinated political commitment among a group of states.
That precedent carries a clear lesson for Bangladesh: International linguistic recognition requires diplomacy, institutional preparedness, and financial commitment in addition to a large speaker population.
The global importance of a language can also be measured through economic and geopolitical influence. Approximately 1.5 billion people worldwide speak English, followed by Mandarin with around 1.1 billion, Hindi with approximately 600 million, Spanish with about 550 million, Arabic with around 370 million, Bengali with approximately 350 million, French with around 270 million, and Russian around 250 million.
But when language is assessed through economic and geopolitical power, the ranking changes. The World Economic Forum's "Power Language Index" places English, Mandarin, French, Spanish, Arabic, Russian, German, Japanese, Portuguese, and Hindi among the world's most influential languages.
The index considers factors such as economic opportunity, access to knowledge and media, geographic diplomacy, travel, and the ability to facilitate dialogue. Bangla's challenge, therefore, is not a lack of speakers. It is the comparatively limited economic and institutional power associated with the language outside its traditional geographic base. That is something Bangladesh can change.
Bangla has already acquired an extraordinary cultural legacy. Rabindranath Tagore became the first Asian Nobel laureate, receiving the Nobel Prize in Literature. Amartya Sen received the Nobel Prize in Economics, while Dr Muhammad Yunus received the Nobel Peace Prize. Bengali literature, music, cinema, and scholarship have continued to attract international audiences.
Bangla-language media have also expanded beyond Bangladesh and India. Bangla programs have been broadcast through radio and television in countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, Russia, Germany, China, Japan, the Philippines, Iran, and Pakistan. Bengali newspapers and online media platforms are published across the world, while the use of Bangla on the internet has grown significantly.
UN Radio launched Bangla-language programming in 2012, although the service was suspended in 2021 amid budget constraints during the Covid-19 pandemic. The UNDP has also published its annual report on Asia in Bangla alongside the English edition.
Meanwhile, Bangladesh's diplomatic community has been using language as a form of cultural diplomacy. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs organizes events in Dhaka to mark International Mother Language Day, with representatives of foreign missions participating. Diplomats posted in Bangladesh pay tribute to the language martyrs by laying flowers at a temporary Shaheed Minar at the Foreign Service Academy.
Some foreign diplomats posted in Dhaka have also taken up learning Bangla. These developments demonstrate that the internationalization of Bangla is already taking place, albeit incrementally and without a sufficiently coordinated strategy.
For Bangla to become an official language of the United Nations, Bangladesh would need to formally place the issue before the General Assembly and seek support for a resolution.
Such an initiative would require extensive diplomatic engagement with other member states. But diplomacy should not begin with the resolution. It should begin much earlier. It is worth noting that Bangladesh is presiding over the current session of the United Nations General Assembly.
Bangladesh would first need to build a broad coalition of countries and international organizations willing to support the initiative. It would need to demonstrate that the financial and technological requirements of incorporating Bangla into the UN system can be met.
It would also need to establish a credible institutional mechanism for translation, interpretation, terminology development, and quality control. Most importantly, the government would need to treat the issue as a long-term state policy rather than an occasional diplomatic initiative.
There is no simple population-based formula for determining which languages become official UN languages. The existing six official languages themselves demonstrate that geopolitical history, diplomatic influence, and international utility have played a major role.
Bangla is one of South Asia's major languages. Its history is inseparable from one of the world's most significant struggles for linguistic rights. Its literature has produced globally recognized figures. Its speakers span continents. Its digital presence is expanding. And its symbolic importance has already been acknowledged by the international community through International Mother Language Day.
Bangla has a history worthy of international recognition. But the question is whether Bangladesh can convert that historical and cultural capital into sustained diplomatic, technological, and economic influence.
Recognition at the United Nations would undoubtedly carry symbolic importance. It could enhance the international visibility of Bangla, strengthen Bangladesh's cultural identity, and make communication between Bengali speakers and international institutions easier.
But official recognition alone would not guarantee the global expansion of a language. Languages thrive when people have reasons to learn and use them.
That means Bangladesh must simultaneously increase the economic, technological, and cultural value of Bangla. Electronic and digital media can play a major role. Bengali cinema, drama, music, literature, publishing, educational content, software, and AI applications can all contribute to expanding the language's global reach.
The commercialization of Bangla should not be seen as a threat to its cultural identity. Rather, economic utility can reinforce cultural influence. A language that becomes useful in education, technology, entertainment, business, and international communication is more likely to cross borders and attract new learners. This is perhaps the most important lesson for Bangladesh.
The struggle for Bangla began with a demand for linguistic dignity. It evolved into a defining element of national identity.
The next stage requires a different kind of movement -- one built not only on emotion and historical memory, but also on diplomacy, technology, investment, cultural production, and economic opportunity.
Seventy years after Bangla became the state language of Pakistan's eastern wing and more than seven decades after the Language Movement, Bangladesh has an opportunity to take the language's global journey to another level.
Making Bangla an official language of the United Nations may be a long and difficult process. It may require years of diplomacy, substantial investment, and considerable institutional preparation. But the ambition itself is neither unrealistic nor misplaced.
If Bangladesh wants Bangla to speak more prominently on the world stage, it must first give the language the economic, technological, and diplomatic strength to be heard. The time has come to move from commemorating the language to strategically investing in its future.
Salahuddin Ahmaad Bablu is a senior journalist.

item.title: AI didn't give me sight. It gave me independence. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A few months ago, I received a phone call from a mother who is blind. She was not calling to discuss technology. She was calling because she was worried about her two-year-old son.
"My son has learned that I cannot see," she told me. "He has also learned that if he stays completely quiet, I cannot find him. Sometimes he hides in a corner of the room without making a sound. Those are the moments that frighten me the most."
As she spoke, I could hear something that every parent understands: Fear for a child's safety. But for her, that fear was magnified by the simple reality that she could not rely on vision.
I suggested she try an AI-powered visual assistance app. Using the smartphone's camera, the app analyzes the surroundings and describes them aloud in real time.
A few weeks later, she called me again.
This time, her voice sounded different.
"My phone tells me, 'Your child is standing near the door.' It says, 'Your child is playing with a toy.' Sometimes it even tells me what he is holding. I can find him almost immediately."
The technology had not restored her eyesight.
But it had restored something equally important: Confidence.
That conversation stayed with me because it perfectly captured what artificial intelligence really means for many persons with disabilities.
Public discussions about AI usually focus on automation, productivity, investment, or whether machines will replace human jobs. Those conversations are important. Yet they often overlook another reality.
For millions of people with disabilities, AI is not about replacing people. It is about reducing dependence.
I know this because I live it every day.
I am a person with a visual disability, and for much of my life, ordinary tasks depended on someone else's availability.
If someone handed me a printed document, I had to ask them to read it.
If I received a business card, I had to ask whose name was written on it.
If I wanted to identify the label on a medicine bottle or read information on product packaging, I often needed another person's help.
There is nothing wrong with asking for support. We all depend on one another in different ways.
But when every simple task requires assistance, independence slowly slips away.
Artificial intelligence is changing that.
Today, I begin my mornings by reading the news independently. AI reads newspapers and online articles aloud, allowing me to follow national affairs, global events, and public debates without waiting for someone else to read them to me.
When I prepare for work, AI helps identify the colour of my clothes and suggests matching combinations.
To many people, choosing a shirt may seem insignificant.
To me, choosing my own clothes without asking another person is dignity in action.
Even this article has been shaped with the help of AI.
I speak, AI converts my words into text, and I refine the ideas. What once took hours can now be accomplished far more efficiently, allowing me to spend less time overcoming barriers and more time contributing my expertise.
Across the world, similar stories are unfolding every day.
Students are accessing textbooks more independently.
Professionals are reviewing documents and writing reports.
Entrepreneurs are managing businesses.
People are navigating unfamiliar places with greater confidence.
Families are communicating more effectively.
AI is quietly removing barriers that many people never realized existed.
However, technology alone is not enough. AI can only be transformative when the digital world itself is accessible.
An intelligent assistant cannot fully compensate for a website that cannot be navigated with a screen reader, an online form that is inaccessible from the keyboard, or a mobile application that ignores basic accessibility standards.
Accessibility remains the foundation. AI is an accelerator -- not a substitute -- for inclusive design.
As someone who has spent more than two decades working on digital accessibility, I see AI as one of the greatest opportunities to build a more inclusive society. But that opportunity will only be realized if governments, businesses, educators, developers, and technology companies intentionally include persons with disabilities in designing and testing digital products.
The disability community has long embraced the principle: "Nothing about us without us."
The same principle must guide the future of AI.
When people with disabilities participate in designing technology, AI becomes more accurate, more useful, and ultimately more human.
People sometimes ask me whether AI has changed my life.
My answer is simple.
AI did not give me sight. It gave me something I value just as much.
The freedom to read independently.
The confidence to make my own choices.
The dignity to participate more equally in society.
And for millions of people with disabilities around the world, that may be AI's most remarkable achievement.
Vashkar Bhattacharjee is a digital accessibility expert and disability rights advocate with a visual disability and over 20 years of experience. Email: vashkarbd@gmail.com .

item.title: The case for digital banks. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank’s initial approval for five digital banks is an encouraging development for the country’s financial sector -- a move that can help accelerate the transition towards a more accessible, technology-driven banking system while creating new opportunities for people who remain underserved by conventional banking channels.
The proposed institutions, backed by businesses including bKash, Robi, Banglalink, and Square Group, will operate without conventional branches, providing banking services primarily through digital platforms.
This model could make financial services more convenient, particularly for people and small businesses that face difficulties accessing traditional banking facilities.
Bangladesh has already experienced rapid growth in mobile financial services, making the expansion of digital banking a natural next step.
There is also considerable potential for digital banks to support smaller borrowers and entrepreneurs: According to Bangladesh Bank, the new institutions are expected to focus on underserved customers and smaller loans rather than large-scale lending.
If managed responsibly, this could help broaden access to formal finance and support economic participation among people who have traditionally remained outside the banking system.
At the same time, innovation must be accompanied by strong safeguards. Digital banking will involve the collection and management of significant amounts of financial and personal data, making cybersecurity, consumer protection, and reliable digital infrastructure essential.
Bangladesh Bank must maintain rigorous oversight to ensure that technological convenience does not come at the expense of financial security or public confidence.
It is also important to remember that an initial approval is not a final license. The proposed banks must establish the necessary infrastructure and fulfil regulatory requirements before they can begin operations. This measured approach is welcome.
If the new banks combine innovation with accountability, security, and responsible lending, they could help make Bangladesh’s financial system more inclusive and efficient.
The move, therefore, represents a potentially important step towards a banking sector that better reflects the country’s increasingly digital economy.

item.title: Putting Bangladesh first. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s address to the 81st United Nations General Assembly was a historic moment for the nation, and we commend how he presented a broad vision for our future.
The speech outlined the values the government says should guide the country’s next chapter: Democracy, equality, accountability, dignity, opportunity, peace, and inclusive development.
The emphasis on rebuilding democratic institutions and ensuring equal rights is particularly significant -- aspiring for a nation where people, regardless of political affiliation, religion, or race, can live safely and with dignity, and where democracy extends across the country.
The focus on young people, women, and children reflects another important part of this vision.
Developing skills, creating employment, encouraging entrepreneurship, expanding women’s education and economic participation, and strengthening education, health and sports could help Bangladesh make better use of its demographic dividend.
If pursued effectively, such priorities could create a society where citizens have greater opportunities to build secure and productive lives.
The speech also placed Bangladesh within a wider global framework: Its calls for peaceful conflict resolution, multilateral cooperation, climate justice, technology transfer, and fair access to artificial intelligence demonstrate an emphasis on cooperation and shared responsibility.
Ultimately, however, the significance of this vision will depend on how firmly these principles take root at home.
Economic inclusion must reach those who have traditionally been left behind. Education and employment opportunities must translate into better prospects for young people, while women and children must be able to benefit from the country’s progress.
The speech has therefore set out an expansive vision of a safer, more democratic, inclusive and self-reliant Bangladesh.
The opportunity now lies in turning that vision into sustained action. If the values outlined at the UN become the foundation of governance and development, they could help shape a future in which progress is measured not only by economic growth, but by how widely security, dignity, and opportunity are shared.
